title: Add Edges to Make Degrees of All Nodes Even
statement:
An undirected graph has `n` nodes labelled `1` to `n`; each `edges[i] = [a_i, b_i]` joins nodes `a_i` and `b_i`. The graph need not be connected.

You may add up to two new edges (zero, one or two). A new edge must join two different nodes and must not duplicate an edge that is already in the graph or another edge you add.

A node's degree is how many edges touch it. Return `true` if some choice of added edges leaves every node with an even degree, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: No edge appears twice (in either direction)
notes:
## Intuition

Every edge changes the degree of exactly two nodes by one, so only the set of odd-degree nodes matters. The number of odd nodes is always even, and two new edges can fix at most four of them. That leaves three cases to check:

- **0 odd nodes**: nothing to add.
- **2 odd nodes `a`, `b`**: join them directly, or, if they are already joined, route through a third node that is joined to neither (its degree rises by 2 and stays even).
- **4 odd nodes**: split them into two pairs and join each pair; there are only three ways to pair four nodes.

More than four odd nodes can never be fixed. Trying every pair of new edges would also work, but it is O(n⁴) pairs.

## Approach

1. Count each node's `degree` and store every edge in the set `linked` in both directions; `free(a, b)` asks whether `a`–`b` is still unused.
2. Collect the nodes with odd degree in `odd`.
3. With none, return `true`.
4. With two, return `true` if `free(a, b)`, or if some other `node` has `free(a, node)` and `free(b, node)`.
5. With four, return `true` if any of the three pairings has both of its edges free.
6. Otherwise return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

Degrees are node 1: 2, node 2: 4, node 3: 2, node 4: 3, node 5: 1, so `odd = [4, 5]`. There is no edge `4`–`5`, so `free(4, 5)` is true and adding it makes every degree even: the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): one pass over the edges, one over the nodes, and at most one more scan in the two-odd case.
- Space: O(n + m) for the degrees and the edge set.

## Pitfalls

- With two odd nodes that are already adjacent, do not give up: a third node joined to neither of them works.
- That third node must differ from `a` and `b`, or the new edge would be a self-loop.
- In the four-odd case, check all three pairings, not just the first one.
- Six or more odd nodes are hopeless: two edges change at most four degrees, so return `false` without searching.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `degree` | number of edges touching each node |
| `linked` | set of existing edges, stored in both directions |
| `free(a, b)` | true when no edge joins `a` and `b` yet |
| `odd` | nodes whose degree is odd |
| `a`, `b`, `c`, `d` | the odd nodes in the 2- and 4-node cases |
| `node` | a candidate third node in the two-odd case |

narration.2: Degrees are counted per node; index 0 is unused because nodes start at 1.
narration.3: A set of existing edges lets us ask in O(1) whether a new edge would be a repeat.
narration.5: Each edge adds one to the degree of both of its ends.
narration.7: Store the edge as a single number in both directions so lookups ignore order.
narration.10: free(a, b) is true when no edge joins a and b yet, so we may add one.
narration.13: Scan every node to find the ones with odd degree.
narration.14: Only odd nodes need fixing; remember them.
narration.17: No odd nodes: the graph already works without adding anything.
narration.18: Two odd nodes: they must both gain an odd number of new edge ends.
narration.20: Joining them directly fixes both at once if that edge is new.
narration.21: Otherwise look for a third node to route two new edges through.
narration.22: A node joined to neither a nor b gains 2 (staying even) while a and b each gain 1.
narration.24: Every possible third node is already adjacent to a or b, so it cannot be done.
narration.26: Four odd nodes: two new edges must pair them up exactly.
narration.28: First pairing: a with b and c with d.
narration.29: Second pairing: a with c and b with d.
narration.30: Last pairing: a with d and b with c; its answer is the final answer.
narration.32: An odd count above four needs more than two edges, so it is impossible.
